desc:
In a binary grid a 1 is land and a 0 is water. An island is a maximal group of land cells connected through the four directions. The grid is called split when it does not contain exactly one island (it has none, or two or more).

In one operation you turn a single land cell into water. Return the minimum number of operations needed to make the grid split. If it is already split, the answer is 0.

grid = [[1,1,1],
        [0,1,0],
        [1,1,1]]   -> 1
grid = [[1,1],
        [1,1]]     -> 2
grid = [[1,0,1]]   -> 0

In the first example removing the middle cell separates the top row from the bottom row.
hints: The answer is always 0, 1 or 2. Try to see why 2 is enough whenever the land is one island.

Answer 0: the grid already has no island or at least two. Answer 1: removing one particular cell splits the land, which means that cell is a cut vertex (articulation point) of the land graph, or the island is a single cell. Otherwise the answer is 2.

Why 2 always works: take the top-most, then left-most land cell. It has at most two land neighbours (right and below). Removing both isolates it, or empties the grid. To check for answer 1, test every land cell by removing it and counting islands (small grids), or find articulation points with one DFS (low-link values).
editorial: Count the islands first. If there is not exactly one, return 0. Otherwise, if the island has a single cell, removing it leaves no land, so the answer is 1.

The answer is at most 2: the top-most, left-most land cell can have land neighbours only to the right and below, so removing at most those two cells isolates it from the rest (or empties the island). Therefore we only have to decide whether one removal is enough. One removal splits the island exactly when the removed cell is an articulation point of the graph whose vertices are the land cells. Compute articulation points with an iterative DFS using discovery times and low-link values: a non-root vertex v is an articulation point if it has a child u with low[u] ≥ disc[v], and the root is one if it has at least two DFS children.
That is O(R · C) time. A simpler approach removes every land cell in turn and recounts the islands, which costs O((R · C)<sup>2</sup>) and is also fine for small grids.
